content: Cannabis sativa is a plant that has been utilized by humans throughout recorded history for various purposes. Its fibers, known as hemp, have been used for textile production, while its oil-bearing seeds have served as a source of nourishment. Additionally, the plant has been valued for its psychological and physiological effects. Different parts of the plant are cultivated and harvested in distinct ways depending on their intended use, and various strains or varieties are grown for specific purposes. Taxonomy and Varieties The taxonomic classification of Cannabis was detailed in 1976 by Ernest Small and Arthur Cronquist, though other taxonomic treatments are also recognized by some botanists. C. sativa subsp. sativa var. sativa The correct name for this taxon is Cannabis sativa L. subsp. sativa var. sativa. This variety includes hemp landraces and cultivars grown primarily for fiber or seed production. Fiber strains are typically tall and unbranched, while seed strains are often shorter and may be either branched or unbranched. Some strains are monoecious, meaning they possess both male and female reproductive organs. Certified industrial hemp strains produce a high ratio of cannabidiol (CBD) to tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), approximately 20:1, making them unsuitable for drug use. C. sativa subsp. sativa var. spontanea The correct name for this taxon is Cannabis sativa L. subsp. sativa var. spontanea (Vavilov) Small & Cronq., with a synonym of C. ruderalis Janisch. This variety includes wild or feral Cannabis plants that have lost many of the traits originally selected for through breeding and have adapted to their local environments. These plants are often short, branchless, and early-flowering, with low levels of cannabinoids and a low THC-to-CBD ratio, rendering them of little use for drug production. However, indica drug strains are sometimes crossbred with ruderalis to produce high-THC plants with the hardiness and reduced height of ruderalis. The term ruderal was originally used in the former Soviet Union to describe escaped hemp populations that had adapted to surrounding regions. These plants are widespread in central and eastern Europe, including Lithuania, Belarus, Latvia, and Estonia, as well as in areas of North America where hemp cultivation was once common. In North America, feral Cannabis is often referred to as ditch weed. Outside its native range, it is considered an invasive species. Despite eradication efforts, these plants remain abundant. Some have proposed recognizing this taxon as a distinct species, C. ruderalis. C. sativa subsp. indica var. indica The correct name for this taxon is Cannabis sativa L. subsp. indica (Lam.) Small & Cronq. var. indica (Lam.) Wehmer, with a synonym of C. indica Lam. This variety includes two types of Cannabis cultivated for drug production, commonly referred to as sativa and indica by Cannabis enthusiasts. Narrow-leafed sativa drug strains and landraces are native to the Indian subcontinent and are also cultivated in Africa, South and Central America, the Caribbean, and other marijuana-producing regions. These strains are typically tall, loosely branched, and late-maturing. They have largely been replaced by indica/sativa hybrids in commercial cultivation due to the hybrids' higher yields and shorter growth cycles. Wide-leafed indica drug strains are traditionally cultivated in northwest India, Afghanistan, and Pakistan for hashish production and may have originated in the Hindu-Kush or Tian Shan mountain ranges. These strains are better suited for temperate climates due to the harsh and variable conditions of their native regions. Plants of this type are relatively short, conical, and densely branched, with wide leaflets. They tend to produce a lower THC-to-CBD ratio than narrow-leafed strains. While many commercially available varieties are bred to produce high THC and low CBD levels, some users report a more stoned and less high effect compared to narrow-leafed strains. Differences in terpenoid content may account for these effects. Anecdotal evidence suggests that sativa strains produce clearer, cerebral highs, while indica strains produce more sedative, body-focused effects, often associated with drowsiness, reduced motor coordination, and increased appetite. No definitive chemical or pharmacological basis for these differing effects has been identified. Some have proposed recognizing this taxon as a distinct species, C. indica. Recent genetic, morphological, and chemotaxonomic analyses have assigned both narrowand wide-leafed drug biotypes, as well as southern and eastern Asian hemp landraces and wild Himalayan populations, to C. indica. C. sativa subsp. indica var. kafiristanica The correct name for this taxon is Cannabis sativa L. subsp. indica (Lam.) Small & Cronq. var. kafiristanica (Vavilov) Small & Cronq., with a synonym of C. indica Lam. var. kafiristanica Vavilov. This variety includes wild or feral plants, primarily found in the Indian subcontinent and other regions where Cannabis is cultivated for drug use and has escaped cultivation. Individual plants may have low, moderate, or high levels of THC relative to CBD. Plants with high levels of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabidivarin (THCV) and/or cannabidivarin (CBDV) are also common in this group. Compared to var. spontanea, plants of this taxon are often taller and more branched, with very small achenes (fruits). The inflorescences of pistillate (female) plants are often elongated, and the fruits drop off the plants as they mature. Common Uses The tough fibers of Cannabis, cultivated as hemp, have numerous applications in textiles. Its seeds, often used as bird feed, are a valuable source of protein. The flowers, and to a lesser extent the leaves, stems, and seeds, contain psychoactive and physiologically active compounds known as cannabinoids, which are consumed for recreational, medicinal, and spiritual purposes. Preparations of flowers (marijuana) and resinous extracts (hashish) are typically consumed by smoking, vaporizing, or oral ingestion. Historically, tinctures, teas, and ointments were also common preparations. Plant Physiology Cannabis reproduces sexually. Female plants produce flowers arranged in racemes, which can yield hundreds of seeds. Male plants shed pollen and die several weeks before seed ripening on female plants. While genetic factors determine whether a plant becomes male or female, environmental factors, such as the light cycle, can influence sexual expression. Naturally occurring monoecious plants, which have both male and female parts, may be sterile or fertile. Artificially induced hermaphrodites can have fully functional reproductive organs. Feminized seeds sold commercially are derived from artificially hermaphroditic females that lack the male gene or are treated with hormones or silver thiosulfate. Cannabis plants in the vegetative growth phase require 18 hours of light and 6 hours of darkness to remain vegetative. Flowering typically occurs when darkness exceeds 12 hours per day, and water is reduced. The flowering cycle lasts between four to six weeks, depending on the strain and environmental conditions. Cannabis thrives in a pH range of 5.5 to 6.5, making it well-suited for hydroponic cultivation, as this pH range inhibits most bacteria and fungi. Pharmacology The primary psychoactive compound in Cannabis is Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), though the plant contains approximately 60 cannabinoids, most of which are produced in trace amounts. Cannabidiol (CBD), another major cannabinoid, is non-psychoactive and has been shown to block THC's effects in the nervous system. Differences in the chemical composition of Cannabis varieties may result in varying effects in humans. Synthetic THC, known as dronabinol, lacks CBD, cannabinol (CBN), and other cannabinoids, which may explain its differing pharmacological effects compared to natural Cannabis preparations. Most commonly available Cannabis contains less than 8% THC, but selective breeding and modern cultivation techniques, such as hydroponics, have produced varieties with THC levels exceeding 15%. Varieties with less than 1% THC, such as those cultivated for hemp, may cause lightheadedness or mild headaches when smoked but do not produce intoxication. Female plants generate significantly more resin than male plants, and seedless floral clusters from unpollinated female plants (known as sinsemilla) typically have higher THC content than seeded inflorescences.
